title: Your First Three Seconds Are Getting Skipped. Fix the Sentence Before the Video.
markdown:
# Your First Three Seconds Are Getting Skipped. Fix the Sentence Before the Video.

The clip is edited. The captions are on. You post it, watch the view count twitch, and then the retention graph drops like it found a trapdoor.

That first dip is painful because it is usually not a camera problem. It is a sentence problem.

People scrolling short-form video do not begin by asking whether your advice is good. They make a faster call: does this open a loop I want closed, or does it sound like the last ten videos? A hook has to earn the next second before your explanation gets a chance.

This is the promise: you can stop treating every opening line as a tiny emergency and build a repeatable way to generate, test, and sharpen them.

## What a swipe-resistant hook actually does

A useful hook gives the viewer a reason to stay without pretending it has already delivered the answer. It creates tension, specificity, or a recognizable mistake. It does not need to yell.

Compare these two openings:

> “Today I want to talk about why your videos are not getting views.”

> “Your video can be useful and still lose the viewer before your first point.”

The second line names a frustrating contradiction. A creator who has made a thoughtful video and watched it disappear recognizes the situation immediately. They now want to know why it happens.

The best hooks tend to start with material already inside the video: the claim that surprised you, the mistake that cost time, the before-and-after, or the objection a skeptical viewer will have. The hook is not decoration added at the end. It is the front door to the actual point.

## Stop asking for “a viral hook”

“Make this viral” is too vague to be useful. It invites loud, generic lines that could introduce almost any video. A better brief tells the writer what the video changes for someone and what makes the change hard to believe.

Before you write an opening, collect four raw ingredients:

- Who is this for, in ordinary language?
- What are they trying to do?
- What keeps going wrong at the moment?
- What is the one detail in your video that makes your answer credible or unexpected?

For a video about product photography, “small shop owners whose photos look flat under indoor light” is more usable than “entrepreneurs.” For a video about editing, “the cut that makes a tutorial feel slow before the first example” beats “editing tips.” Specificity gives you something to pull on.

Then make several openings with different jobs. One can challenge a familiar assumption. Another can put a costly mistake in plain sight. A third can start with the result and hold back the method for the next beat. You are looking for a line that matches the video you made, not a line that would work on a stranger’s account.

## A practical test before you record again

Read the hook aloud without the rest of the script. If it needs the next sentence to make basic sense, rebuild it. If it could introduce a hundred unrelated clips, add the detail only your video has.

Next, ask a harsher question: would the intended viewer feel seen, challenged, or curious in the first breath? If the honest answer is “maybe,” keep working. A mild opening asks the viewer to donate attention. A strong one gives them a reason.

Do not confuse mystery with vagueness. “You will not believe this” hides the subject. “I stopped using the feature everyone recommends after it doubled my editing time” makes a claim the viewer can evaluate. The second line has a real destination.

Finally, make sure the video pays off the opening early. A hook can win a pause and still damage trust if the useful part arrives too late. Give the viewer a concrete example, a demonstration, or the first step soon after the premise. Retention is not a trick contest; it is a promise kept at the right speed.

## Turn the blank-page moment into a repeatable process

You do not need to summon a brilliant sentence on command. You need a prompt that makes you supply the right raw material, then returns options you can judge against the actual footage.

Hook Lab is built for that moment. Feed it the audience, the subject, the tension, and the proof inside the video, then choose an opening you would genuinely say on camera. It is especially useful when you have a solid script but keep rewriting the first line until the posting window passes.

Get the ready-to-use Hook Lab prompt here: https://promptbase.com/prompt/hook-lab-win-the-first-3-seconds-2?via=keipanda&ct=capafy-distribute-promptbase-hook-lab

The goal is not to sound like every high-performing clip. It is to give the right viewer a precise reason to stop, then make the rest of the video worth that pause.
